data.text/markdown:
Growing a minimum spanning tree

Connect every pair of points. The cheapest set of lines that still links them all is the minimum spanning tree. Two classic ways to grow one:
  • Prim: grow one tree outward from a start point.
  • Kruskal: take edges shortest-first, merging small trees into one.
Press play, or drag the timeline to scrub.

Prim: one tree grows outward

Pop the cheapest edge leaving the tree (blue), add its far end, push that point's edges (orange). Stale edges get skipped (red). Timeline: heap size.

Kruskal: a forest merges

Walk the edges shortest-first. Keep one that joins two fragments, skip one that would close a cycle (red). Timeline: number of fragments.

Or use the geometry

For points on a plane, the MST always lies on the Delaunay triangulation: about 3n edges instead of n²/2. So build that first, then run Kruskal on it.
  1. Triangulate, starting from one huge helper triangle around everything. Each new point: find the triangles whose circle holds it (red), cut them out, fan new ones from the point (blue). The view zooms in as points arrive; the helper's corners (dashed) are dropped at the end.
  2. Kruskal on the triangle edges only: blue is the current edge, red dashed would close a cycle.
Checking every triangle for every new point makes this slow (1.6 s at 1,600 points), so the benchmark builds the same triangulation with scipy, in C.

Which one is faster?

The same functions race on two graphs:
  • complete: every pair linked, up to 1,600 points
  • sparse: 6 nearest neighbours each, up to 102,400 points
Plus Prim without a heap (a plain list of the cheapest edge to each point, scanned every round) and, on the complete graph, Delaunay + Kruskal. Anything slower than half a second per run drops out. Takes ~30 s, so it waits for the button.

data.text/markdown:
• Complete graph: no-heap Prim wins. Each edge is one list update for it. The heap version pushes 1.28M edges at 1,600 points to use 1,599; Kruskal sorts them all first.
  • Sparse graph: no-heap Prim still scans all n points each round, so it drops out early. Heap Prim and Kruskal tie.
  • Points on a plane: skip the complete graph. Delaunay + Kruskal finds the same tree at 1,600 points in ~6 ms, against ~160 ms for the best of the rest.
Dense graph: scan a list. Sparse graph: use a heap or a sort.

When does Kruskal win?

1. Islands. Prim stops at the edge of its own island. Kruskal returns one tree per island, for free.
